# Verifying Account Ecosystems With Graph Transformations

##### Murphy, F.; Radomirovic, S.

#### Proceedings - 11th European Symposium on Security and Privacy, EuroS and P 2026: 470-490

#### 2026

* * *

ISSN/ISBN: 9798319510747

DOI: 10.1109/eurosp68448.2026.00038
Accession: 109526523

##### Summary

Account ecosystems comprise a set of resources, including online accounts, devices, and credentials, that jointly impact a user's or organisation's security. Prior work shows that users frequently overlook subtle dependencies within these ecosystems, leading to security breaches that are difficult to detect using analysis techniques focused on isolated components.We introduce resource access graphs (RAGs), a formal model for the automated analysis of dynamic account ecosystems. RAGs extend previous work on account access graphs (AAGs) with partially ordered labels for vertices and edges, enabling both general and resource-specific actions to be modelled. To capture the dynamic nature of account ecosystems, we define a transition system based on graph rewriting with RAGs as states in which both user actions and adversarial capabilities are modelled as graph transformation rules.

L49: ## Abstract
L50: We develop a research agenda for the field of automata learning. Automata learning algorithms infer state-machines from observations. The study of such algorithms began in the 1970s and until today has led to a wide range of different learning models, learnability results, and learning algorithms for many different classes of automata as well as to many different applications of automata learning, e.g., specification generation, learning-based testing, and black-box verification.
L51: As the field still stratifies and learning algorithms and new applications are conceived, it will be helpful to consolidate and integrate individual obtained results into a coherent set of principles of automata learning and techniques for devising learning algorithms.
L52: We aim to provide a step in this direction by conducting a survey of active automata learning methods, focusing on different application scenarios (application domains, environments, and desirable guarantees) and the overarching challenges that emerge from these. We identify concrete research questions through a (short) bibliographic study highlighting the state of the art and the technical implications that are derived from the overarching challenges.

L41: ###### Abstract
L42: Safety is still one of the major research challenges in reinforcement learning (RL). In this paper, we address the problem of how to avoid safety violations of RL agents during exploration in probabilistic and partially unknown environments. Our approach combines automata learning for Markov Decision Processes (MDPs) and shield synthesis in an iterative approach. Initially, the MDP representing the environment is unknown. The agent starts exploring the environment and collects traces.
L43: From the collected traces, we passively learn MDPs that abstractly represent the safety-relevant aspects of the environment. Given a learned MDP and a safety specification, we construct a shield. For each state-action pair within a learned MDP, the shield computes exact probabilities on how likely it is that executing the action results in violating the specification from the current state within the next $k$ steps.
L44: After the shield is constructed, the shield is used during runtime and blocks any actions that induce a too large risk from the agent. The shielded agent continues to explore the environment and collects new data on the environment. Iteratively, we use the collected data to learn new MDPs with higher accuracy, resulting in turn in shields able to prevent more safety violations. We implemented our approach and present a detailed case study of a Q-learning agent exploring slippery Gridworlds.
L45: In our experiments, we show that as the agent explores more and more of the environment during training, the improved learned models lead to shields that are able to prevent many safety violations.
L46: ###### Keywords:
L47: 
L48: Automata Learning Shielding Markov Decision Processes
L49: ## 1 Introduction
L50: Nowadays systems are increasingly autonomous and make extensive use of machine learning. The tremendous potential of autonomous, AI-based systems is contrasted by the growing concerns about their safety [【27†11】]. Their huge complexity makes it infeasible to formally prove their correctness or to cover the entire input space of a system with test cases. An especially challenging problem is ensuring safety during the learning process [【28†21】].
L51: In model-free reinforcement learning (RL) [【29†34】], an agent aims to learn a task through trial-and-error via interactions with an unknown environment. While the model-free RL approach is very general as well as scalable and has successfully been applied in various challenging application domains [【30†20】], the learning agent needs to explore unsafe behavior in order to learn that it is unsafe.
L52: Shielding [【31†4】] is a runtime enforcement technique that applies correct-by-construction methods to automatically compute shields from a given safety temporal logic specification [【32†5】] and a model that captures all safety-relevant dynamics of the environment. Shields have been categorized into post-shields and pre-shields. Post-shields monitor the actions selected by the agent and overwrite any unsafe action with a safe one.
L53: Pre-shields are implemented before the agent and block, at every time step, unsafe actions from the agent (also referred to as action masking). Thus, the agent can only choose from the set of safe actions. In this paper, we use pre-shielding since this setting allows the agent maximal freedom in exploring the environment.
L54: In the non-probabilistic setting [【33†6】], shields guarantee that the safety specification will never be violated, working under the assumption that a complete and faithful environmental model of the safety-relevant dynamics is available. Shielding in the probabilistic setting [【34†19】], which is the standard setting in RL, assumes to have an environmental model in form of a Markov decision process (MDP) available.
L55: Given such an MDP $\mathcal{M}$ and a safety specification $\varphi$, the shield computes how likely it is that executing an action from the current state will result in violating $\varphi$ within a given finite horizon. At any state $s$, an actions $a$ is called unsafe if executing $a$ incurs a probability of violating $\varphi$ within the next $k$ steps greater than a relative threshold $\lambda$ w.r.t. the optimal safety probability possible in $s$.
L56: The resulting shield prohibits safety violations that can be prevented by planning ahead $k$ steps into the future. Shielding requires a complete and accurate environmental model, but it is rarely the case that such a model is available. However some data about the environment often exists, for example, a RL agent collects data by exploring the environment.
L57: Automata learning [【35†38】, 【36†1】, 【37†17】] is a well-established technique to automatically learn automata models of black-box systems from observed data. The data used for automata learning is usually given in the form of observation traces, which are sequences of observations of the environment’s state and actions chosen by the agent. Passive MDP learning [【38†23】, 【39†24】] is able to learn MDP models from a multiset of sampled observation traces.
L58: Thus, the learned MDP depends on the given sampled traces.
L59: Our approach. In this paper, we consider the setting of RL in an initially unknown environment. The goal is to reduce safety violations during the exploration phase of the RL-agent by combining passive MDP learning with probabilistic shielding in an iterative approach. Initially, the MDP representing the environment is unknown. During runtime, the agent collects observation traces while exploring the environment.
L60: After having a large enough initial multiset of traces, we first transform the sequences of observed states in the traces into observations, which include only the safety-relevant information, using a suitable abstraction function. The abstract traces are then used to learn a first estimate of the safety-relevant MDP. From this initial MDP and a given safety specification, we construct an initial shield.
L61: After the shield is constructed, the agent is augmented with the shield, i.e., the shield blocks unsafe actions from the agent and the agent can pick from the set of safe actions. The newly collected traces are added to the multiset of all traces. After collecting a predefined number of new traces, our approach learns a new safety-relevant MDP from the multiset of all collected traces and creates a new shield.
L62: At every iteration, the shield is built from an MDP that approaches more and more the real MDP underlying the environment modulo the abstraction to safety-relevant observations. Thus, the resulting shields are getting more informed and prevent the agent from entering more safety-critical situations.
L63: Outline. The rest of the paper is structured as follows. We present the related work in Section 【7†2】 and discuss the relevant foundations in Section 【8†3】. We present our approach for safe learning via shielding and automata learning in Section 【12†4】. We present our experimental results in Section 【16†5】 and conclude in Section 【24†6】.
L64: ## 2 Related Work
L65: We combine automata learning and probabilistic verification to create safety shields in our approach. Early work on such combinations has been performed by Cobleigh et al. [【40†10】], who propose to learn assumptions for compositional reasoning. More closely related to our work is black box checking by Peled et al. [【41†31】], where they present a technique for model checking of deterministic black-box systems.
L66: Learning-based testing by Meinke and Sindhu [【42†26】] follows a similar approach of incremental learning of hypothesis models and model checking of these hypotheses. In previous work [【43†3】], we proposed a technique inspired by black box checking for probabilistic reachability checking of stochastic black-box systems. As in this paper, we applied IOAlergia [【38†23】, 【39†24】] to learn MDPs. Rather than computing safety shields from learned MDPs, we computed policies to satisfy reachability objectives.
L67: We also proposed a technique for $L^{*}$-based learning of MDP [【44†35】], which may serve as a basis for RL and shielding. In this paper, we combine stochastic learning and abstraction with respect to safety-relevant features to improve RL. Nouri et al. [【45†30】] also apply abstraction on traces with respect to properties of the system under consideration in order to learn abstract probabilistic models.
L68: In contrast to us, they aim to improve the runtime of statistical model-checking and they learn Markov chains that are not controllable via inputs.
L69: Recently, various authors have proposed combinations of automata learning and reinforcement learning [【46†14】, 【47†42】, 【48†18】, 【49†13】]. By learning finite-state models, such as so-called reward machines, they provide additional high-level structure for RL. This enables RL when rewards are non-Markovian, i.e., the gain depends not only on the current state and action, but on the path taken by the agent. DeepSynth [【50†16】] follows a similar approach to improve RL with sparse rewards.
L70: Related to these approaches, Muskardin et al. [【51†29】] propose a combination of reinforcement learning and automata learning to handle partial observability, i.e., non-Markovian environments.
L71: Fu and Topcu [【52†12】] presented an approach for a learning-based synthesis of policies for MDPs w.r.t. temporal logic specifications that are probably approximately correct. In contrast to us, they assume the topology of the MDP to be known, so that only transition probabilities need to be learned.
L72: Alshiekh et al. [【31†4】] proposed shielding for RL. Jansen et al. [【34†19】] proposed the first method to compute safety shields using a bounded horizon in MDPs. Giacobbe et al. [【53†15】] applied the same technique on 31 Atari 2600 games. The approach was further extended by Könighofer et al. [【54†22】]. Instead of analyzing the safety of all state-action pairs ahead of time, the approach uses the time between two successive decisions of an agent to analyze the safety of actions on the fly. Pranger et al.
L73: [【55†33】] proposed an iterative approach to shielding that updates the transition probabilities of the MDP based on observed behavior and computes new shields in regular intervals. To construct our shields, we use the approach proposed by Jansen et al. [【34†19】]. Similarly to Pranger et al. [【55†33】], we iteratively construct new shields, but do not rely on a known topology of the MDP.
L74: As in our approach, Waga et al. [【56†40】] use automata learning to dynamically construct shields during runtime. The main difference to our work is that they assume that the environment behaves deterministically, whereas we allow probabilistic environmental behavior which is the standard assumption in reinforcement learning.
L75: ## 3 Preliminaries
L76: ##### Basics.
L77: Given a set $E$, we denote by $\mathit{Dist}(E)$ the set of probability distributions over $E$, i.e. for all $\mu$ in $\mathit{Dist}(E)$ we have $\mu:E\rightarrow[0,1]$ such that $\sum_{e\in E}\mu(e)=1$. In Section 【12†4】, we apply two randomized functions $\mathit{coinFlip}$ and $\mathit{randSel}$. The function $\mathit{coinFlip}$ is defined by $\mathbb{P}(\mathit{coinFlip}(p)=\top)=p$ and $\mathbb{P}(\mathit{coinFlip}(p)=\bot)=1-p$ for $p\in[0,1]$.
L78: The function $\mathit{randSel}$ samples an element $e$ from a given set $E$ according to uniform distribution, i.e., $\forall e\in E:\mathbb{P}(\mathit{randSel}(E)=e)=\frac{1}{|E|}$.
L79: ### 3.1 Markov Decision Processes and Reinforcement Learning
L80: ###### Definition 1
L81: 
L82: A Markov decision process (MDP) is a tuple $\langle\mathcal{S},s_{0},\mathcal{A},\mathcal{P}\rangle$ where $\mathcal{S}$ is a finite set of states, $s_{0}\in\mathcal{S}$ is the initial state, $\mathcal{A}$ is a finite set of actions, and $\mathcal{P}:\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}\rightarrow\mathit{Dist}(\mathcal{S})$ is the probabilistic transition function.
L83: For all $s\in\mathcal{S}$ the available actions are $\mathcal{A}(s)=\{a\in\mathcal{A}\>|\>\exists s^{\prime},\mathcal{P}(s,a)(s^{\prime})\neq 0\}$ and we assume $|\mathcal{A}(s)|\geq 1$. We associate an MDP $\mathcal{M}$ with a reward function $\mathcal{R}:\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}\times\mathcal{S}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}$.
L84: Traces. A finite path $\rho$ through an MDP is an alternating sequence of states and actions, i.e. $\rho=s_{0}a_{1}s_{1}\cdots a_{n-1}s_{n-1}a_{n}s_{n}\in s_{0}\times(\mathcal{A}\times\mathcal{S})^{*}$. The set of all paths of an MDP $\mathcal{M}$ is denoted by $Path_{\mathcal{M}}$. We refer to a path augmented with the gained reward as a reward trace $\tau=s_{0}a_{1}r_{1}s_{1}\cdots s_{n-1}a_{n}r_{n}s_{n}$ with $r_{i}=\mathcal{R}(s_{i-1},a_{i},s_{i})$.

L4@P0: Safe exploration is a common problem in reinforcement learning (RL) that aims to prevent agents from making disastrous

L9@P0: applications, one must look beyond enforcing safety and also
L10@P0: ensure the applicability of RL with good performance. We
L11@P0: extend the applicability of shields via tight integration with
L12@P0: state-of-the-art deep RL, and provide an extensive, empirical
L13@P0: study in challenging, sparse-reward environments under partial observability. We show that a carefully integrated shield
L14@P0: ensures safety and can improve the convergence rate and final
L15@P0: performance of RL agents. We furthermore show that a shield
L16@P0: can be used to bootstrap state-of-the-art RL agents: they remain safe after initial learning in a shielded setting, allowing
L17@P0: us to disable a potentially too conservative shield eventually.
L18@P0: 1 Introduction
L19@P0: Reinforcement learning (RL) (Sutton and Barto 1998) is a
L20@P0: technique for decision-making in uncertain environments.
L21@P0: An RL agent explores its environment by taking actions
L22@P0: and perceiving feedback signals, usually rewards and observations on the system state. With success stories such as
L23@P0: AlphaGo (Silver et al. 2016) RL nowadays reaches into areas such as robotics (Kober, Bagnell, and Peters 2013) or
L24@P0: autonomous driving (Sallab et al. 2017).
L25@P0: A significant limitation of RL in safety-critical environments is the high cost of failure. An RL agent explores the
L26@P0: effects of actions – often selected randomly, such as in stateof-the-art policy-gradient methods (Peters and Schaal 2006) –
L27@P0: and will thus inevitably select actions that potentially cause
L28@P0: harm to the agent or its environment. Thus, typical applications for RL are games (Mnih et al. 2013) or assume the
L29@P0: ability to learn on high-fidelity simulations of realistic scenarios (Tao et al. 2019). The problem of unsafe exploration has
L30@P0: triggered research on the safety of RL (Garcıa and Fernandez ´
L31@P0: 2015). Safe RL may refer to (1) changing (“engineering”) the
L32@P0: reward function (Laud and DeJong 2003) to encourage the
L33@P0: agent to choose safe actions, (2) adding a second cost function

L36@P0: (“constraining”) (Moldovan and Abbeel 2012), or (3) blocking (“shielding”) unsafe actions at runtime (Alshiekh et al.
L37@P0: 2018). This paper falls into the last category.
L38@P0: Safe RL in partially observable environments suffers from
L39@P0: uncertainty both in the agent’s actions and perception. Such
L40@P0: problems, typically modeled as partially observable Markov
L41@P0: decision processes (POMDPs) (Kaelbling, Littman, and Cassandra 1998), require histories of observations to extract a
L42@P0: sufficient understanding of the environment. Recent deep RL
L43@P0: approaches for POMDPs, including those that employ recurrent neural networks (Hausknecht and Stone 2015; Wierstra et al. 2007), learn from these histories and can generate
L44@P0: high-quality policies with sufficient data. However, these approaches do not guarantee safety during or after learning.
L45@P0: While shielding for Markov decision processes (MDPs) is
L46@P0: rather well-studied (Konighofer et al. 2017; Alshiekh et al. ¨
L47@P0: 2018; Fulton and Platzer 2018; Bouton et al. 2019), there is—
L48@P0: to the best of our knowledge—no approach that integrates
L49@P0: shielding with deep RL.
L50@P0: We contribute a thorough study, implementation, and experimental evaluation on integrating state-of-the-art RL for
L51@P0: POMDPs with shields. We demonstrate effects and insights
L52@P0: using several typical examples and provide detailed information on RL performance as well as videos showing the
L53@P0: exploration and training process. In particular, we integrate
L54@P0: various RL algorithms from Tensorflow (Guadarrama et al.
L55@P0: 2018) with a shield that guarantees safety regarding so-called
L56@P0: reach-avoid specifications, a special case of temporal logic
L57@P0: constraints (Pnueli 1977). The computation of the shields is

L61@P0: POMDP, while probabilities and rewards may remain unspecified (Raskin et al. 2007).

L950@P12: 6.1 Model expressivity
L951@P12: Since the introduction of active automata learning for DFAs,
L952@P12: there have been numerous extensions of 𝐿∗-type algorithms
L953@P12: to other types of (automata) models. A classical extension
L954@P12: is to Mealy machines, which provide a natural yet simple
L955@P12: model for input-output behaviour, and is standard in automata
L956@P12: learning. However, there have been extensions to much richer
L957@P12: features such as automata with data and time, to succinct
L958@P12: representations, quantitative features, and much more. We
L959@P12: do not give a comprehensive overview of these extensions,
L960@P12: instead focusing on several research challenges.

L963@P12: inference of rich, multi-faceted systems?
L964@P12: Data languages and register automata A first class of
L965@P12: extensions is to data languages, which feature infinite alphabets, and are relevant to capture various types of resources
L966@P12: and data. A classical automata model recognising these languages is that of register automata.
L967@P12: There are several algorithms for active learning of register automata [3, 39, 95] and the related model of nominal
L968@P12: automata [126, 127]. This is an ongoing line of research,
L969@P12: and a recent result improves on the complexity of learning
L970@P12: register automata by using classification tree-based learning

L972@P12: the underlying tree queries remains an open challenge. At

L974@P12: produce symbolic representations of residual data languages

L316: Rather than authorizing decryption in the abstract, SUDP authorizes a specific secret-backed operation together with its redemption binding and validity conditions. L50: ## Abstract
L51: Partially-Observable Markov Decision Processes (POMDPs) are a well-known stochastic model for sequential decision making under limited information. We consider the EXPTIME-hard problem of synthesising policies that almost-surely reach some goal state without ever visiting a bad state. In particular, we are interested in computing the winning region, that is, the set of system configurations from which a policy exists that satisfies the reachability specification.
L52: A direct application of such a winning region is the safe exploration of POMDPs by, for instance, restricting the behavior of a reinforcement learning agent to the region. We present two algorithms: A novel SAT-based iterative approach and a decision-diagram based alternative. The empirical evaluation demonstrates the feasibility and efficacy of the approaches.

L16: > Abstract:Agentic systems now act with user secrets for APIs, messaging platforms, and cloud services. Today's agent runtimes typically implement authorization by exposure: enabling action means placing a reusable secret, or a reusable artifact derived from it, inside the runtime, so a transient prompt-injection or tool-side compromise becomes durable account compromise.
L17: Existing defenses cover adjacent pieces such as secret storage, scoped delegation, sender-constrained tokens, and runtime monitoring, but none states the combined requirement: an untrusted autonomous requester should be able to cause a user-authorized secret-backed operation without gaining reusable authority over it. We formalize this as the Agent Secret Use (ASU) problem and identify seven security properties any solution must satisfy, spanning authorization integrity and secret confidentiality.
L18: We propose the Secret-Use Delegation Protocol (SUDP), in which a requester proposes a canonical operation, the user authorizes it with a fresh authenticator-backed grant, and a custodian redeems the grant to perform the bounded use; reusable authority never crosses the requester boundary. We specialize SUDP for LLM-driven agents, where it applies whenever a tool call would exercise user-enrolled authority-bearing material.
L19: Under standard cryptographic assumptions, SUDP satisfies six of the seven properties; the seventh, runtime-memory confidentiality, is closed by composition with a hardware-rooted runtime. A reference implementation, available at 【12†this https URL†github.com】, adds sub-millisecond protocol overhead per mediated call.

L71: ## Abstract
L72: Security verification of communication protocols in industrial and safety-critical systems is challenging because implementations are often proprietary, accessible only as black boxes, and too complex for manual modeling. As a result, existing security testing approaches usually depend on incomplete test suites and/or require labor-intensive modeling, limiting coverage, scalability, and trust.
L73: This paper addresses the problem of systematically verifying protocol security properties without access to internal system models. We propose a flexible and scalable method for formal verification of communication protocols that combines active automata learning with model checking to enable rigorous security analysis of black-box protocol implementations. Behavioral models are first inferred from system interactions using automata learning.
